lesson_1.title: Data Structures: Array Initialization
task: An array is a foundational data structure that stores a sequence of elements in contiguous memory.
Initializing a fixed-size array is an O(1) constant time operation because the system allocates a single, continuous block of memory regardless of the specific numerical values contained.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `create_basic_array`.
2. Utilize the array creation construct to instantiate a new array.
3. Populate the array with exactly three integer values: 10, 20, and 30.
4. Return the initialized array. The static analyzer will verify this sequence as an O(1) constant time operation.

lesson_1.title: Constant-Time Metadata Evaluation
task: In modern data structures, determining the size of an array does not require sequentially counting each element.
The array maintains its length as internal metadata. Retrieving this pre-calculated metadata is an O(1) constant-time algorithmic operation.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `get_list_length(arr)`.
2. Retrieve the built-in length evaluation operator.
3. Apply the operator to the `arr` parameter.
4. Return the resulting integer to demonstrate constant-time metadata access.

lesson_1.title: Constant-Time Index Access
task: Arrays utilize zero-based indexing to determine the position of elements. Because arrays occupy contiguous memory, the system can mathematically calculate the exact memory address of any element instantly.
Consequently, accessing an array element by its index is an O(1) constant time operation.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `get_first_item(arr)`.
2. Implement a defensive conditional check to verify if the list is empty. If true, return the integer `0`.
3. If the array contains elements, utilize the index access block to retrieve the item located at index 0.
4. Return the retrieved item.

lesson_1.title: In-Place Memory Mutation
task: Standard arrays are mutable data structures, meaning their contents can be modified after initialization.
Updating an element at a specific index overwrites the existing memory block. This is an in-place operation that requires O(1) time and allocates O(1) auxiliary space.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `update_first_element(arr)`.
2. Implement a boundary check to ensure the array is not empty. If it is empty, return the unmodified `arr`.
3. Utilize the index assignment block to modify the element at index 0.
4. Assign the integer `99` to this position.
5. Return the updated `arr` structure.

lesson_1.title: Dynamic Array Appending
task: Dynamic arrays are engineered to expand their memory allocation sequentially. Appending an element to the tail of the array is highly efficient.
Because it does not require shifting existing elements, this operation executes in amortized O(1) constant time.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `add_to_end(arr, item)`.
2. Retrieve the standard list append block.
3. Configure the block to append the parameter `item` to the parameter `arr`.
4. Return the modified `arr` structure.

lesson_2.title: State Accumulation: Summation
task: Algorithms frequently utilize iterative traversal combined with a state tracking variable to aggregate data.
We will construct a linear O(n) summation algorithm by traversing an array and continuously modifying an accumulator variable.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `sum_array(arr)`.
2. Initialize an accumulator variable named `total` and assign it the integer `0`.
3. Construct a standard iteration loop to traverse each element within `arr`.
4. Within the loop, apply an addition operation to increment the `total` variable by the current element's value.
5. Return the finalized `total` variable.

lesson_2.title: Linear Traversal: Finding Extrema
task: To determine the maximum value within an unsorted dataset, an algorithm must evaluate every element sequentially against a recorded maximum state.
This extrema-finding algorithm executes in strict O(n) linear time.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `find_max(arr)`.
2. Implement a defensive condition: if `arr` is empty, return `0`.
3. Initialize a variable named `max_val` and assign it the value located at `arr[0]`.
4. Construct a loop to iteratively traverse the array elements.
5. Within the loop, evaluate if the current element is strictly greater than `max_val`.
6. If the condition is true, update `max_val` to equal the current element.
7. Return the `max_val` variable.

lesson_2.title: Conditional State Tracking
task: Algorithms often require executing isolated logic blocks strictly when specific dataset conditions are met.
We will integrate linear array traversal with conditional mathematics to isolate and count targeted elements.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `count_evens(arr)`.
2. Initialize an accumulator variable named `count` to 0.
3. Construct a standard loop to traverse the parameter `arr`.
4. Inside the loop, utilize the modulo operator to evaluate if the current element divided by 2 yields a remainder of 0.
5. If the condition validates as true, increment the `count` variable by 1.
6. Return the `count` variable.

lesson_2.title: Linear Search: Sequential Traversal
task: To determine if a specific value exists within an unsorted dataset, an algorithm must evaluate each element sequentially.
This algorithm, formally known as Linear Search, yields an O(n) time complexity. The algorithm optimizes operational efficiency by terminating the iteration immediately once the target is identified.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `contains_item(arr, target)`.
2. Construct an iterative loop to traverse each element in `arr`.
3. Implement a conditional check to evaluate if the current element is strictly equal to the `target`.
4. If the condition evaluates to true, execute an early exit by immediately returning `True`.
5. If the iteration concludes without a match, return `False`.

lesson_2.title: Data Transformation (Mapping)
task: In algorithm design, we rarely just copy data. Instead, we transform it while moving it. This process is called 'Mapping'.
Let's map an array by creating a new list where every original number has been mathematically doubled.
Instructions:
1. Define `double_array(arr)`.
2. Create a new empty list called `result`.
3. Use a 'for each item' loop to iterate over `arr`.
4. Inside the loop, do not just append the item. Open the 'Math' tab, grab a multiplication block, and append `item * 2` to `result`.
5. Return the newly transformed `result` list.

lesson_3.title: Constant-Time Deletion (Pop)
task: Removing an element from the very end of a dynamic array is highly efficient.
Because no remaining elements need to be shifted to close a memory gap, executing a tail deletion resolves in O(1) constant time.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `remove_last_item(arr)`.
2. Implement a defensive evaluation. If the array is empty, return the string 'Empty'.
3. Locate the built-in function to remove and retrieve the final item from a sequence.
4. Apply this function to the `arr` parameter.
5. Return the retrieved item.

lesson_3.title: In-Place Array Reversal
task: Algorithms that modify data without allocating new structures are classified as 'in-place'. They operate with an optimal O(1) auxiliary space complexity.
We will invert the sequence of an array directly within its existing memory footprint.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `reverse_in_place(arr)`.
2. Initialize two pointers: `left = 0` and `right = len(arr) - 1`.
3. Construct a `while` loop that continues as long as `left < right`.
4. Within the loop, apply an in-place swap operation to exchange the values at `arr[left]` and `arr[right]`.
5. Increment the `left` pointer and decrement the `right` pointer to converge toward the center.
6. Return the modified `arr`.

lesson_3.title: Quadratic Space: 2D Array Allocation
task: Data structures are not limited to a single dimension. When an algorithm allocates an array within another array recursively or iteratively, the spatial footprint scales quadratically.
We will construct an N x N matrix to demonstrate O(n²) space complexity.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `create_matrix(n)`.
2. Initialize an empty array named `matrix`.
3. Construct an outer loop configured to iterate `n` times.
4. Inside the outer loop, initialize a new empty array named `row`.
5. Construct an inner loop, also configured to iterate `n` times.
6. Inside the inner loop, append the integer `0` to the `row` array.
7. After the inner loop concludes, append the completed `row` to the `matrix`.
8. Return the `matrix`.

lesson_3.title: Time-Space Tradeoff: In-Place Deletion
task: Algorithm design often requires balancing time and space efficiency. Removing an element from an array without allocating a new list operates in optimal O(1) auxiliary space.
However, this forces a time-space tradeoff. Because contiguous memory cannot have empty gaps, the system must shift all subsequent elements, degrading the operation to O(n) linear time.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `remove_target(arr, target)`.
2. Utilize the native list operation to remove the first occurrence of the `target` value from `arr`.
3. Return the modified `arr` structure.
4. Observe the static analyzer. The syntax is concise, but the structural memory shift enforces an O(n) time complexity alongside the O(1) space complexity.

lesson_3.title: Memory Overhead: Array Slicing
task: Extracting a contiguous sub-section of an array using slicing operators often appears to be a lightweight procedural step.
Algorithmically, slicing allocates an entirely new array in memory and duplicates the elements into it. This operation yields an O(n) space complexity overhead.
Instructions:
1. Define the function `extract_tail(arr)`.
2. Implement a defensive conditional check to verify the array possesses at least 3 elements. If it does not, return an empty array `[]`.
3. Utilize the array slicing operator to extract elements from index 1 to the end of the array.
4. Return the newly allocated sub-array to demonstrate linear space scaling.

optimizations.title: Optimization Challenge: In-Place Reversal
task: Reversing an array by creating a secondary list requires additional memory allocation, resulting in an O(n) space complexity overhead.
We can optimize this algorithm to operate with O(1) auxiliary space by mutating the original array in-place utilizing two converging pointers.
Optimization Guidelines:
1. Eliminate the initialization of the secondary storage array.
2. Initialize two pointer variables: `left` assigned to 0, and `right` assigned to `len(arr) - 1`.
3. Construct a `while` loop constrained by the logical evaluation `left < right`.
4. Implement an in-place swap operation to exchange the values currently residing at `arr[left]` and `arr[right]`.
5. Increment the `left` pointer and decrement the `right` pointer to converge toward the array center.
6. Return the modified `arr` structure. Observe the analyzer register the optimal O(1) space complexity.

optimizations.title: Optimization Challenge: Running Totals
task: Computing a running total by repeatedly calculating the sum from the initial index forces the algorithm to utilize nested loops. This architectural flaw degrades performance to an O(n²) time complexity.
We can optimize this process to O(n) linear time by eliminating the inner loop and maintaining a continuous running accumulator during a single sequential traversal.
Optimization Guidelines:
1. Delete the nested iterative loop structure entirely.
2. Initialize an accumulator variable `current_sum` to 0, alongside an empty `result` array.
3. Construct a single sequential loop to traverse the parameter array.
4. During each iteration, increment `current_sum` by the current element's mathematical value.
5. Append the updated `current_sum` state to the `result` array.
6. Return the `result` array. The analyzer will mathematically verify the optimization to O(n) time complexity.

optimizations.title: Optimization Challenge: Mathematical Series
task: Iterating sequentially through a numerical sequence to aggregate a total sum incurs a mandatory O(n) linear time complexity.
When evaluating the sum of a contiguous numerical sequence, computer scientists leverage standard mathematical formulas to replace iterative loops, achieving an optimal O(1) constant time complexity.
Optimization Guidelines:
1. Remove the iterative loop construct and the accumulator variable from the workspace.
2. Implement the arithmetic series formula utilizing the `n` parameter: `(n * (n + 1)) / 2`.
3. Return the computed formula result.
4. The static analyzer evaluates direct mathematical substitutions as constant-time operations, confirming your algorithm now executes in O(1) time.
